questions.question: Is 2 a quadratic residue mod 7?
options: Yes, since 2 = 3² mod 7 (9 mod 7 = 2)
No, since no x in {1,…,6} satisfies x² ≡ 2 (mod 7)
Yes, since 2 is itself a square in the integers (√2 is real)
No, since only odd residues can be squares modulo primes p > 2
questions.explanation: 3² = 9 ≡ 2 (mod 7). Also 4² = 16 ≡ 2. So 2 is a QR mod 7.

questions.question: How many quadratic residues exist in `(Z/pZ)*` for an odd prime p?
options: p, since every residue squares to something in the field
(p − 1)/2, since x and −x square to the same value
p − 1, half the field plus an extra from the identity element
(p + 1)/2, including zero as a quadratic residue by convention
questions.explanation: Map x ↦ x² is 2-to-1 on (Z/pZ)* since x and −x have the same square. So exactly (p−1)/2 distinct non-zero QRs.

questions.question: Euler's criterion identifies QRs how?
options: a is a QR mod p iff a^((p−1)/2) ≡ 1 (mod p); otherwise it ≡ −1
a is a QR mod p iff a^(p−1) ≡ 1 (mod p) by Fermat's little theorem
a is a QR mod p iff a divides p − 1 cleanly without remainder
a is a QR mod p iff gcd(a, p−1) = 1 in the multiplicative group
questions.explanation: Euler's criterion: a^((p−1)/2) ≡ +1 (mod p) if a is a QR, ≡ −1 if non-QR (a ≠ 0, p odd prime).

questions.question: Tonelli-Shanks computes what?
options: Modular inverse a⁻¹ mod p when gcd(a, p) = 1 in logarithmic time
Square root x with x² ≡ a (mod p) when a is a quadratic residue
Discrete log x with g^x ≡ a (mod p) for a given generator g
Primitive root g such that g generates (Z/pZ)* of full order p − 1
questions.explanation: Tonelli-Shanks: given a QR a mod p, find x with x² ≡ a (mod p). Handles all odd primes; runs in O(log² p).

questions.question: For p ≡ 3 (mod 4), modular square root has a closed form. What is it for QR a?
options: x ≡ a^((p+1)/4) (mod p), which avoids Tonelli-Shanks's loop entirely
x ≡ a^((p−1)/2) (mod p), giving the Euler criterion value as root
x ≡ a^((p+1)/2) (mod p), one extra exponentiation beyond Euler
x ≡ a^(p−2) (mod p), the Fermat-inverse-based fallback for roots
questions.explanation: When p ≡ 3 (mod 4), x = a^((p+1)/4) mod p. Check: x² = a^((p+1)/2) = a · a^((p−1)/2) ≡ a · 1 = a (mod p).

questions.question: Find a square root of 3 mod 11 (i.e. x with x² ≡ 3).
options: x = 4, since 4² = 16 ≡ 5 (mod 11) which differs from 3
x = 6, since 6² = 36 = 33 + 3 ≡ 3 (mod 11) ✓ same as ±5
x = 7, since 7² = 49 ≡ 5 (mod 11) which is not the target

questions.question: Why is square-root mod a composite n = p·q believed to be as hard as factoring?
options: Computing four roots mod pq via CRT requires p, q separately, and recovering distinct ±r mod p and ±s mod q yields gcd(r−s, n) = a factor
Square roots mod composites do not exist; the problem is provably unsolvable for all composite n
Tonelli-Shanks succeeds mod composites only when n is a Carmichael number, which is rare for RSA
Quadratic residue testing mod composites equals discrete log, which is harder than factoring asymptotically
questions.explanation: A square-root oracle gives you both √a (mod p) and (mod q). Two random independent roots r, s with r² ≡ s² ≡ a give gcd(r ± s, n) = p or q. Used in Rabin cryptosystem.

questions.question: Goldwasser-Micali encryption uses QR hardness mod composite n. What does the attacker need to distinguish to break it?
options: Square roots from non-square roots — equivalent to computing them outright
QRs from QNRs with Jacobi symbol +1 — believed hard without factoring n
Even-indexed residues from odd-indexed ones in the cyclic subgroup
Primes p from composites n efficiently — requires polynomial-time AKS
questions.explanation: Quadratic Residuosity Problem: given a with Jacobi(a/n)=+1, decide if a is a true QR mod n=pq or a pseudosquare. Believed as hard as factoring.
